china_race_dynamics.text: Every time we get down to the nub of the question, can these giant corporations take the copyrighted work of individual citizens, we get distracted with, well, it is for the good of the country, maybe it is not so bad, we have an arms race on, there is an AI czar. [...] I think in America, we have rights. Those rights are what protect us. These rights are being violated. And if we are going to succeed as a nation and uphold our principles as a nation, we better darn well enforce the individual rights on which the nation is founded.
china_race_dynamics.context: Senate Judiciary Subcommittee hearing on the AI industry's use of copyrighted works for AI training, chaired by Senator Hawley questioning Professor Lee.

deepseek.reason: The speaker dismisses the AI arms race as a distraction from enforcing individual rights.
deepseek.confidence_reason: The race-skeptical language is explicit, but China is not named, leaving target identity somewhat uncertain.

astra.reason: The speaker rejects arms-race excuses for copyright violations but does not identify competition with China.
astra.confidence_reason: Neither the statement nor its context establishes that the arms race refers to China.

china_race_dynamics.text: The Chinese government also uses artificial intelligence, AI, for the troves of data it collects on its own citizens every day, particularly on ethnic minorities like the Uighers, against whom the Chinese government is committing human rights abuses.
china_race_dynamics.context: Senate floor speech by Senator Dick Durbin advocating for the U.S. Innovation and Competition Act (USICA), citing China's AI-enabled surveillance as a national security concern.

deepseek.reason: The statement criticizes China's AI surveillance but does not address making competition with China a US policy priority.
deepseek.confidence_reason: The text is a China criticism without an explicit US competition-priority stance.
